newsitem.title: CHINA: KFC beating local firm in Shanghai chicken war.
newsitem.headline: KFC beating local firm in Shanghai chicken war.

text.p: In Shanghai's fast-food chicken war, the American bird is winning and the Chinese bird is down but not out.

Since December 1989, Kentucky Fried Chicken (KFC) has opened 24 outlets in China's biggest city, with a turnover of 250 million yuan ($30 million) in the first half of 1996, double that of a year earlier.
It plans 100 outlets in Shanghai by the end of the century.

In comparison, the biggest local competitor, Ronghuaji (Glorious China Chicken), has seven outlets in Shanghai and 10 nationwide, with expected 1996 sales of about 60 million yuan, similar to the 1995 level.
Its lacklustre performance contrasts sharply with China's overall fast-food industry, which is a golden goose.
In 1995, total fast-food turnover with 280,000 outlets was 30 billion yuan, accounting for 25 percent of the country's food and drink business, the Economic Daily reported.
Foreign producers, especially KFC and McDonald's, have led the way, with advertising, standards of quality, management and cleanliness that Chinese competitors have been unable to match.
KFC's success in Shanghai is typical.

"I come here twice a week," said Wang Mei, a 25-year-old insurance agent nibbling at five pieces of chicken costing 32 yuan ($3.86) in a KFC outlet with 360 seats on Nanjing Road, Shanghai's busiest shopping street.

"The taste is better and more consistent than Ronghuaji," she said. "When Ronghuaji opened here, people queued to buy it. But its quality has slipped and the company seems to be on its way down. Ronghuaji's chicken is too greasy."
"We come here for my son," said a factory worker, watching his son tuck in while he smoked a cigarette. "My wife and I do not like this kind of food, but he does. So we come often."

Industry analysts ascribe KFC's success to its early entry into the market, the taste of Shanghai people for fried chicken, a high standard of cleanliness, good service and heavy advertising and promotion, much of it aimed at children.
In August, Shanghai KFC spent 1.14 million yuan on 181 television advertisements on local channels, ranking it the second biggest advertiser for the month.

"We came early, in 1989, and many foreign and domestic fast-food companies followed us," Liu Jiulong, chairman of KFC-Shanghai, said in an interview. "Shanghai people are more willing (than other Chinese) to accept foreign goods. KFC made good use of this opportunity."
Shanghai KFC is 49 percent owned by Shanghai New Asia and 51 percent by Pepsi Restaurant International, a unit of PepsiCo Inc.
Nationwide, KFC expects to have 500 outlets in China by the year 2000, up from the current 112, with sales in the first half 1996 of one billion yuan.
Its first and biggest local competitor was Ronghuaji, a Shanghai state company, which set up copycat chain shops in Shanghai and Beijing close to KFC, offering similar products.

"It is not exactly equal competition," said Hu Xinquan, a senior official of Ronghuaji, sipping orange juice in one of their shops in downtown Shanghai. "We are a six-year-old child in the business and KFC is a 60-year-old veteran."
"KFC has levels of capital we cannot match. They advertise heavily on television while we are doing no television advertising this year," he said.
"Much of their advertising is aimed at children, with toys and promotions," he said. "It is the children who bring the parents to KFC. Parents want to make their children happy."
He said Ronghuaji wants to open three more outlets in Shanghai next year, bringing its network in the city to 10.
"Competition in the fast food market is fierce. Near one of our stores on Nanjing Road there are five other fast food shops, both foreign and local," he said.

China's fast-food industry is handicapped by a lack of common standards, inadequate capital to buy equipment and a tendency to use cheap labour instead of advanced machines, the official Economic Daily said in a critique of the industry.
Most fast-food companies are small and do not have enough money to buy the equipment they need, the newspaper said. Others set standards for their food but do not stick to them.
Most Chinese fast-food companies also have too many items on their menus, making it difficult for consumers to choose, and making delivery of the food "slow" rather than "fast", it said.
